title: Gentrification & Displacement
text:
Gentrification — the process by which higher-income residents move into lower-income neighborhoods, raising rents and changing neighborhood character — is one of the most contested topics in urban economics. The central question: does gentrification displace existing residents?


The process typically unfolds as follows:

A low-rent neighborhood becomes attractive to higher-income households (proximity to jobs, cultural amenities, architecture, or simply affordability relative to other neighborhoods)
Newcomers move in, increasing demand for housing
Rents and property values rise
For renters, higher rents mean higher housing costs. Some can’t afford to stay and leave (displacement). For owners, rising values are a wealth gain.
Commercial activity shifts to serve the new, higher-income population. The neighborhood changes.




The evidence on displacement is surprisingly mixed:

Vigdor (2002) and McKinnish, Walsh, and White (2010) find modest displacement effects. Most incumbent residents in gentrifying neighborhoods don’t move at higher rates than comparable residents in non-gentrifying areas.
Ellen and O’Regan (2011) find that incumbents who stay benefit from improved amenities — better schools, lower crime, cleaner streets.
Brummet and Reed (2019) follow original residents with census data. Gentrification raises moving out only a little, movers are not observably worse off, and many who stay benefit from lower poverty around them.
Ding, Hwang, and Divringi (2016) find that displacement effects are concentrated among vulnerable populations: renters, the elderly, racial minorities, and those with lower credit scores.

The puzzle: gentrification clearly changes neighborhoods, but the displacement channel is hard to detect empirically. This may be because (a) displacement is modest, (b) it’s concentrated in subpopulations, or (c) it’s hard to distinguish from normal mobility.






The Identification Challenge. Measuring displacement requires knowing the counterfactual: would residents have moved anyway? High-mobility populations (renters, young adults) move frequently regardless of gentrification. The simulation below lets you see how rent increases, tenure type, and rent control policy interact to produce displacement over time. See also: Difference-in-Differences for how researchers compare gentrifying vs non-gentrifying neighborhoods.

title: Gentrification & Displacement
text:
Gentrification — the process by which higher-income residents move into lower-income neighborhoods, raising rents and changing neighborhood character — is one of the most contested topics in urban economics. The central question: does gentrification displace existing residents?


The process typically unfolds as follows:

A low-rent neighborhood becomes attractive to higher-income households (proximity to jobs, cultural amenities, architecture, or simply affordability relative to other neighborhoods)
Newcomers move in, increasing demand for housing
Rents and property values rise
For renters, higher rents mean higher housing costs. Some can’t afford to stay and leave (displacement). For owners, rising values are a wealth gain.
Commercial activity shifts to serve the new, higher-income population. The neighborhood changes.




The evidence on displacement is surprisingly mixed:

Vigdor (2002) and McKinnish, Walsh, and White (2010) find modest displacement effects. Most incumbent residents in gentrifying neighborhoods don’t move at higher rates than comparable residents in non-gentrifying areas.
Ellen and O’Regan (2011) find that incumbents who stay benefit from improved amenities — better schools, lower crime, cleaner streets.
Brummet and Reed (2019) follow original residents with census data. Gentrification raises moving out only a little, movers are not observably worse off, and many who stay benefit from lower poverty around them.
Ding, Hwang, and Divringi (2016) find that displacement effects are concentrated among vulnerable populations: renters, the elderly, racial minorities, and those with lower credit scores.

The puzzle: gentrification clearly changes neighborhoods, but the displacement channel is hard to detect empirically. This may be because (a) displacement is modest, (b) it’s concentrated in subpopulations, or (c) it’s hard to distinguish from normal mobility.






The Identification Challenge. Measuring displacement requires knowing the counterfactual: would residents have moved anyway? High-mobility populations (renters, young adults) move frequently regardless of gentrification. The simulation below lets you see how rent increases, tenure type, and rent control policy interact to produce displacement over time. See also: Difference-in-Differences for how researchers compare gentrifying vs non-gentrifying neighborhoods.

title: Gentrification & Displacement
text:
The policy landscape
Gentrification policy typically targets one of two goals: preventing displacement or ensuring existing residents benefit from neighborhood improvements:

Rent stabilization limits annual rent increases, protecting long-term tenants. But it can reduce housing supply (landlords convert to condos or disinvest) and doesn’t protect new tenants.
Community land trusts remove land from the speculative market, ensuring permanently affordable housing. Successful examples include the Champlain Housing Trust (Burlington, VT).
Inclusionary zoning requires developers to include affordable units in new construction. This creates mixed-income neighborhoods but may reduce overall housing supply.
Right of first refusal gives existing tenants or community organizations the right to purchase buildings before they’re sold to outside investors.

No policy is a free lunch. The fundamental tension: neighborhood improvement benefits existing residents (lower crime, better amenities), but the associated rent increases can price them out.

title: Gentrification & Displacement
text:
Connections

Hedonic Pricing — gentrification shows up in hedonic regressions as rising implicit prices for neighborhood amenities (safety, walkability, restaurant access).
Zoning & Housing Supply — inelastic housing supply amplifies rent increases from gentrification. In elastic-supply cities, new construction absorbs demand and rents rise less.
Difference-in-Differences — researchers study gentrification’s effects by comparing gentrifying neighborhoods (treated) to similar neighborhoods that didn’t gentrify (control), relying on parallel trends.
Tiebout Sorting — gentrification is Tiebout sorting at the neighborhood level within a city, rather than across jurisdictions.

title: Gentrification & Displacement
text:
Did you know?

The term “gentrification” was coined by sociologist Ruth Glass in 1964, describing the process in London: “One by one, many of the working class quarters of London have been invaded by the middle classes… Once this process of ‘gentrification’ starts in a district it goes on rapidly until all or most of the original working class occupiers are displaced.”
Measuring displacement empirically is notoriously difficult. The problem is that high-mobility populations (renters, young adults) move frequently regardless of gentrification. To isolate the causal effect of gentrification on out-migration, you need to know the counterfactual — would these residents have moved anyway? Most studies find that the difference between mobility rates in gentrifying vs non-gentrifying neighborhoods is small, which is why the evidence on displacement is so mixed.
Community land trusts (CLTs) are one of the few mechanisms that can permanently decouple housing costs from land speculation. The CLT owns the land and leases it to homeowners, who own only the structure. When they sell, a resale formula limits the price appreciation, keeping the home affordable for the next buyer. One of the largest CLTs in the US, the Champlain Housing Trust in Burlington, VT, has kept homes affordable through multiple housing booms.

title: Gentrification & Displacement
text:
Key papers

Vigdor, J. L. (2002). Does Gentrification Harm the Poor?. Brookings-Wharton Papers on Urban Affairs 2002. Who is displaced.
McKinnish, T., Walsh, R. and White, T. K. (2010). Who Gentrifies Low-Income Neighborhoods?. Journal of Urban Economics 67(2). Who moves in.
Brummet, Q. and Reed, D. (2019). The Effects of Gentrification on the Well-Being and Opportunity of Original Resident Adults and Children. Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia Working Paper 19-30. Effects on original residents.
Asquith, B. J., Mast, E. and Reed, D. (2023). Local Effects of Large New Apartment Buildings in Low-Income Areas. Review of Economics and Statistics 105(2). New market-rate buildings lower nearby rents.

title: Place-Based Policy
text:
Most social programs help people wherever they live. Place-based policies help a place instead. Examples include tax breaks for firms in poor areas, wage subsidies for local workers, and big public projects like dams and highways. The goal is to lift struggling areas.
The hard question is who actually gains. Money aimed at a place does not stay with the people who were there.


Suppose a zone pays a subsidy to everyone who works there. Wages after the subsidy go up, so the zone becomes more attractive. Two forces then kick in:

People move in. If workers can move easily, new workers arrive to claim the subsidy.
Rents rise. More people compete for the same housing. If housing supply is tight, rents go up a lot.

Higher rents eat into the subsidy. Who ends up with the gains depends on two numbers:

Worker mobility. The more easily workers move in, the more the subsidy is spread across newcomers and pushed into rents.
Housing supply elasticity. The easier it is to build, the less rents rise, and the more the subsidy stays with workers.

When workers are mobile and housing is tight, landlords capture most of the gain. This is the core lesson of the Spatial Equilibrium model applied to policy.




Empowerment Zones gave firms wage credits for hiring zone residents. Jobs and wages for residents rose (Busso, Gregory and Kline 2013).
The Tennessee Valley Authority raised manufacturing in the region for decades, but much of that growth moved from other places (Kline and Moretti 2014).
Opportunity Zones barely moved house prices in the zones (Chen, Glaeser and Wessel 2023).







The Model View. A zone pays a subsidy to workers. You set the subsidy, how easily workers move in, and how easily housing gets built. The model finds the new population and rent. The bars show how much of the subsidy ends up with incumbent workers and how much with landlords.

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  w0 <- 50      # wage, $ thousands per year
  r0 <- 15      # rent, $ thousands per year
  u0 <- w0 - r0 # what workers get elsewhere

  solve_zone <- function(s, eta, kappa) {
    rent <- function(N) r0 * N^(1 / kappa)           # N is population relative to start
    # migration: population grows with the zone's advantage over elsewhere
    gap <- function(N) N - exp(eta * ((w0 * (1 + s) - rent(N)) - u0) / u0)
    N <- if (eta == 0) 1 else uniroot(gap, c(0.5, 50))$root
    r <- rent(N)
    list(N = N, r = r,
         worker_gain = w0 * s - (r - r0),     # per incumbent worker
         landlord_gain = r - r0,              # per incumbent unit
         cost = w0 * s * N)                   # subsidy paid per original worker
  }

  model <- reactive(solve_zone(input$sub / 100, input$mob, input$hse))

  output$bars <- renderPlot({
    m <- model()
    s <- input$sub / 100
    vals <- c(w0 * s, m$worker_gain, m$landlord_gain)
    par(mar = c(6, 4.5, 3, 1))
    b <- barplot(vals, col = c("#7f8c8d", "#27ae60", "#e74c3c"),
                 names.arg = c("Subsidy per\nworker", "Incumbent\nworker gain", "Landlord gain\nper unit"),
                 ylab = "$ thousands per year", main = "Who gets the subsidy?",
                 ylim = c(min(0, vals) - 1, max(10, 1.2 * max(vals))))
    abline(h = 0)
    text(b, vals + 0.4, sprintf("%.1f", vals), cex = 0.9)
  })

  output$curve <- renderPlot({
    par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
    ks <- seq(0.1, 5, length.out = 60)
    s <- input$sub / 100
    share <- sapply(ks, function(k) {
      m <- solve_zone(s, input$mob, k)
      if (s == 0) NA else 100 * m$worker_gain / (w0 * s)
    })
    plot(ks, share, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#27ae60", ylim = c(0, 100),
         xlab = "Housing supply elasticity", ylab = "% of subsidy kept by incumbent workers",
         main = "Easier building, more for workers")
    abline(v = input$hse, lty = 3, col = "#2c3e50", lwd = 2)
  })

  output$info <- renderUI({
    m <- model()
    s <- input$sub / 100
    kept <- if (s == 0) "n/a" else paste0(round(100 * m$worker_gain / (w0 * s)), "%")
    tags$div(class = "info-box",
      HTML(paste0(
        "<b>Population change:</b> ", sprintf("%+.0f", 100 * (m$N - 1)), "%<br>",
        "<b>Rent:</b> $", sprintf("%.1f", m$r), "k (was $", r0, "k)<br>",
        "<b>Share kept by incumbent workers:</b> ", kept, "<br>",
        "<b>Subsidy cost per original worker:</b> $", sprintf("%.1f", m$cost), "k"
      ))
    )
  })
}

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  u0 <- w0 - r0 # what workers get elsewhere

    gap <- function(N) N - exp(eta * ((w0 * (1 + s) - rent(N)) - u0) / u0)

    r <- rent(N)

         landlord_gain = r - r0,              # per incumbent unit

  model <- reactive(solve_zone(input$sub / 100, input$mob, input$hse))

title: Place-Based Policy
text:
The case for and against
For: Some people cannot easily move, because of family, home ownership, or cost. Helping their place may be the only way to reach them.
Against: Gains often go to landowners, and activity may just move from one place to another.
The simulation shows one design lesson. Policies tied to people who already live there keep more of the gains with those people than policies that reward anyone who shows up.

title: Place-Based Policy
text:

The Tennessee Valley Authority was created by Congress in 1933 as part of the New Deal. It built dams across the region to supply power and control floods.

title: Segregation and the Schelling Model
text:
US cities are highly segregated by race and income. A natural guess is that this requires strong preferences: people who refuse to live near anyone different. Thomas Schelling showed in 1971 that this guess is wrong. Even mild preferences can produce sharp segregation.


Picture a city as a big square made of small squares. Each small square is one house. In the simulation the city is 40 squares across and 40 squares down, so it has 1,600 houses.
A blue or orange square is a house where a family lives. There are two types of families, blue and orange. A white square is an empty house.
A family’s neighbors are the 8 houses touching its house: left, right, above, below, and the four corners. This is Schelling’s own rule. He wrote that “a convenient minimum-sized neighborhood for an individual is his own square plus the eight surrounding.” A family is happy if at least a share \(T\) of its neighbors are its own color. If not, it moves to a random empty house.
The key is that \(T\) can be low. A family with \(T = 0.35\) is fine being in the minority. It only wants about a third of its neighbors to be like it. Yet when everyone acts on this mild rule, the city sorts into large blocks of one type.



Each move changes the neighborhood for others. When one orange family leaves a mostly blue block, the remaining orange families there now have fewer orange neighbors. Some of them become unhappy and leave. This is a chain reaction, or tipping. No one wants full segregation, but the sum of individual choices produces it.



The simulation uses Schelling’s measure: the share of a family’s 8 neighbors with its own color. Studies of real cities often use the dissimilarity index instead. Split the city into small areas and compare where each group lives. The index is the share of either group that would have to move to make every area match the citywide mix. 0 means fully even. 1 means complete separation. Large US metro areas often have black-white dissimilarity of 0.5 or higher.






The Model View. Set the tolerance threshold and the share of empty houses. Press Run until settled and watch families move, one round at a time. Or press Step to go one round at a time yourself.
The dark box in the middle shows one family’s neighborhood: its house plus the 8 houses touching it. Every house has a neighborhood like this.
The chart below the city tracks segregation using Schelling’s own measure: the average share of each family’s 8 neighbors that have its color. The dashed line is what each family wants. The dotted line is where the city starts: with families placed at random and half of them blue, about half of anyone’s neighbors share its color just by chance. Change the share of blue families to change the starting mix. Watch the average climb far above both.

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  n <- 40      # 40 x 40 grid

  new_grid <- function() {
    e <- input$empty
    g <- sample(c(0L, 1L, 2L), n * n, replace = TRUE,
                prob = c(e, (1 - e) * input$blue, (1 - e) * (1 - input$blue)))
    matrix(g, n, n)
  }

  # count neighbors of each type (wraps around the edges)
  shift <- function(m, dr, dc) {
    r <- ((seq_len(n) - 1 + dr) %% n) + 1
    c <- ((seq_len(n) - 1 + dc) %% n) + 1
    m[r, c]
  }
  like_share <- function(g) {
    same <- matrix(0, n, n); occ <- matrix(0, n, n)
    for (dr in -1:1) for (dc in -1:1) {
      if (dr == 0 && dc == 0) next
      s <- shift(g, dr, dc)
      occ <- occ + (s > 0)
      same <- same + (s == g & g > 0)
    }
    ifelse(occ > 0, same / occ, 1)
  }
  unhappy <- function(g) (g > 0) & (like_share(g) < input$thresh)

  like_avg <- function(g) mean(like_share(g)[g > 0])   # avg share of a family's 8 neighbors with its color

  step_once <- function(g) {
    movers <- which(unhappy(g))
    if (length(movers) == 0) return(g)
    movers <- movers[sample.int(length(movers))]
    for (m in movers) {
      empties <- which(g == 0)
      dest <- empties[sample.int(length(empties), 1)]
      g[dest] <- g[m]; g[m] <- 0L
    }
    g
  }

  state <- reactiveValues(g = NULL, rounds = 0, D = numeric(0))

  init <- function() {
    state$g <- new_grid(); state$rounds <- 0
    state$D <- like_avg(state$g)
  }
  observeEvent(list(input$reset, input$empty, input$blue), init(), ignoreNULL = FALSE)

  advance <- function(k) {
    g <- state$g
    for (i in seq_len(k)) {
      g <- step_once(g)
      state$D <- c(state$D, like_avg(g))
    }
    state$g <- g; state$rounds <- state$rounds + k
  }
  observeEvent(input$step, advance(1))

  # "Run": move one round at a time so you can watch, and stop once no one wants to move
  running <- reactiveVal(FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$run, running(TRUE))
  observeEvent(list(input$reset, input$empty, input$blue), running(FALSE))
  observe({
    req(running())
    invalidateLater(250)
    isolate({
      if (!any(unhappy(state$g)) || state$rounds >= 200) running(FALSE) else advance(1)
    })
  })

  output$grid <- renderPlot({
    req(state$g)
    par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 0.5))
    plot(NULL, xlim = c(0.5, n + 0.5), ylim = c(-4, n + 0.5), asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
         xlab = "", ylab = "", main = paste0("City after ", state$rounds, " rounds"))
    image(1:n, 1:n, state$g, col = c("#ffffff", "#2980b9", "#e67e22"), zlim = c(0, 2), add = TRUE)
    rect(0.5, 0.5, n + 0.5, n + 0.5, border = "#bdc3c7")
    # one example neighborhood: the 3 x 3 square of 9 houses around the center house
    cx <- n / 2; cy <- n / 2
    segments(c(cx - 0.5, cx + 0.5), cy - 1.5, c(cx - 0.5, cx + 0.5), cy + 1.5, col = "#2c3e50", lwd = 1)
    segments(cx - 1.5, c(cy - 0.5, cy + 0.5), cx + 1.5, c(cy - 0.5, cy + 0.5), col = "#2c3e50", lwd = 1)
    rect(cx - 1.5, cy - 1.5, cx + 1.5, cy + 1.5, border = "#2c3e50", lwd = 3)
    legend(n / 2 + 0.5, -0.8, xjust = 0.5, yjust = 1, horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.85,
           x.intersp = 0.8, xpd = TRUE,
           legend = c("Blue family", "Orange family", "Empty house", "Neighborhood (9 houses)"),
           pch = c(22, 22, 22, 0), pt.cex = c(2, 2, 2, 2.6), pt.lwd = c(1, 1, 1, 3),
           pt.bg = c("#2980b9", "#e67e22", "#ffffff", NA), col = c("#7f8c8d", "#7f8c8d", "#7f8c8d", "#2c3e50"))
  })

  output$path <- renderPlot({
    req(state$g)
    par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
    plot(seq_along(state$D) - 1, 100 * state$D, type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2,
         col = "#2c3e50", ylim = c(0, 100),
         xlab = "Round", ylab = "% of neighbors with the same color",
         main = "Segregation over time")
    abline(h = 100 * input$thresh, lty = 2, col = "#e67e22", lwd = 2)
    abline(h = 100 * state$D[1], lty = 3, col = "#7f8c8d", lwd = 2)   # level at the random start
    legend("bottomright", bty = "n", cex = 0.9,
           legend = c("What families get (average)", "What each family wants (T)", "By chance (random start)"),
           col = c("#2c3e50", "#e67e22", "#7f8c8d"), lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = 2, pch = c(19, NA, NA))
  })

  output$info <- renderUI({
    req(state$g)
    g <- state$g
    ls <- like_share(g)[g > 0]
    tags$div(class = "info-box",
      HTML(paste0(
        "<b>Rounds:</b> ", state$rounds,
        if (state$rounds > 0 && !any(unhappy(g))) " (settled: no one wants to move)" else "", "<br>",
        "<b>Unhappy families:</b> ", round(100 * mean(unhappy(g)[g > 0])), "%<br>",
        "<b>Each family wants:</b> ", round(100 * input$thresh), "% like neighbors<br>",
        "<b>Families get, on average:</b> ", round(100 * mean(ls)), "% like neighbors"
      ))
    )
  })
}

Set the share of blue families to 0.8. Blue families start with mostly blue neighbors, but orange families start as a small minority. Many orange families are unhappy from the start, so they move a lot.
Set T = 0. Everyone is happy, no one moves, and the share of like neighbors stays near 50%, what you get by chance.
Set T = 0.75 and run. Many families can never be happy. The city keeps churning and may never settle.

title: Segregation and the Schelling Model
section: From the model to real cities
text:
From the model to real cities
The Schelling model shows that segregation can arise without strong preferences. It does not show that real segregation arose this way. In US history, laws, lending rules, and violence enforced segregation directly. Redlining maps from the 1930s and racial covenants in deeds are well-known examples.
Card, Mas and Rothstein (2008) tested for tipping in real data. They found that once the minority share of a census tract passed a threshold, often between 5% and 20%, the white population tended to fall sharply. The thresholds were higher in cities with more tolerant attitudes.
Segregation matters because neighborhoods shape children’s futures. In the Moving to Opportunity experiment, families got vouchers to move to lower-poverty areas. Chetty, Hendren and Katz (2016) found that children who moved before age 13 earned more as adults. Chetty and coauthors (2022) later found that friendships across income groups are one of the strongest predictors of upward mobility.

title: Segregation and the Schelling Model
text:
Connections

Tiebout Sorting: households also sort by income and taste for public goods.
Gentrification & Displacement: changes in who lives where, seen from the other side.
Crime and Neighborhoods: fear of crime is one reason households move.

title: Segregation and the Schelling Model
text:
Did you know?

Schelling first ran his model by hand, moving coins on a checkerboard. He shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Economics with Robert Aumann.
The dissimilarity index was introduced by Otis Dudley Duncan and Beverly Duncan in 1955. It is still the standard measure in the Census Bureau’s segregation reports.
The model has spread far beyond economics. It is a classic example in computer science and physics of how simple local rules produce large-scale patterns.

title: Segregation and the Schelling Model
text:
Key papers

Schelling, T. C. (1971). Dynamic Models of Segregation. Journal of Mathematical Sociology 1(2). Mild preferences, sharp segregation.
Card, D., Mas, A. and Rothstein, J. (2008). Tipping and the Dynamics of Segregation. Quarterly Journal of Economics 123(1). Tipping points in US neighborhoods.
Gautier, P. A., Siegmann, A. and van Vuuren, A. (2009). Terrorism and Attitudes towards Minorities: The Effect of the Theo van Gogh Murder on House Prices in Amsterdam. Journal of Urban Economics 65(2). After a shocking murder, prices fell in Amsterdam’s minority neighborhoods.
Chetty, R., Hendren, N. and Katz, L. F. (2016). The Effects of Exposure to Better Neighborhoods on Children: New Evidence from the Moving to Opportunity Experiment. American Economic Review 106(4). Moving young pays off.
Chetty, R. and coauthors (2022). Social Capital I: Measurement and Associations with Economic Mobility. Nature 608. Cross-class friendships and upward mobility.

title: Education and Schools
text:
In most of the United States, your address decides your public school. So when families choose a home, they also choose a school. That ties school quality to house prices, and it ties school funding to where people live.


If good schools are worth something, homes in good school zones should cost more. The problem is that good school zones are also nicer in other ways: safer, wealthier, closer to parks. A simple comparison mixes all of these.
Sandra Black (1999) found a clever fix. She compared homes on opposite sides of a school attendance boundary. Homes a block apart share the same neighborhood, but their children go to different schools. Any price gap right at the boundary reflects the schools. She found that a 5% increase in test scores raised house prices by about 2.5%.
This is a regression discontinuity: look only at homes close to the line, where everything but the school is the same.



Schools in rich towns often spend more, because they collect more property tax. For years, economists debated whether more spending actually helps students.
Newer evidence says it does. Jackson, Johnson and Persico (2016) studied court-ordered reforms that sent more money to poor school districts. Children who got more spending finished more school and earned more as adults. The effects were largest for children from low-income families.



Charter schools, vouchers, and open enrollment let some families pick a school without moving. This weakens the link between house prices and schools. It can also change who sorts where, since families no longer have to buy into a district to reach its schools.






The Model View. Homes sit on both sides of an attendance boundary. The school on the right is better. The right side is also a nicer area overall, so prices rise as you move right even without the school. Compare a naive estimate that uses all homes with a boundary estimate that uses only homes near the line.

      HTML(paste0(

title: Education and Schools
text:
Who pays for schools?
US public schools get close to half their money from local sources, mostly property taxes. The rest comes mainly from the state, with a small federal share. Districts with expensive homes can raise a lot of money with a low tax rate. Districts with cheap homes cannot.
Starting in the 1970s, courts in many states ruled that this was unfair. States then sent more money to poorer districts. These school finance reforms are what Jackson, Johnson and Persico used to measure the effect of spending. A 2024 review of many studies by Jackson and Mackevicius finds that more spending raises test scores and college-going on average.

title: Education and Schools
text:
Connections

Tiebout Sorting: families choose towns partly for their schools, and the property tax pays for them.
Hedonic Pricing: school quality is one of the attributes priced into a home.
Segregation and the Schelling Model: sorting by school can deepen segregation by income and race.

title: Education and Schools
text:
Did you know?

Most US public school students attend the school assigned to their home address.
In Serrano v. Priest (1971), the California Supreme Court ruled that funding schools mainly by local property taxes was unfair to students in poor districts. It was one of the first school finance cases.
Real estate listings often name the school zone in the first line. Agents know buyers pay for it.

title: Education and Schools
text:
Key papers

Black, S. E. (1999). Do Better Schools Matter? Parental Valuation of Elementary Education. Quarterly Journal of Economics 114(2). School quality at attendance-zone boundaries.
Bayer, P., Ferreira, F. and McMillan, R. (2007). A Unified Framework for Measuring Preferences for Schools and Neighborhoods. Journal of Political Economy 115(4). What families pay for schools vs neighbors.
Jackson, C. K., Johnson, R. C. and Persico, C. (2016). The Effects of School Spending on Educational and Economic Outcomes: Evidence from School Finance Reforms. Quarterly Journal of Economics 131(1). More spending, more schooling and higher earnings.
Jackson, C. K. and Mackevicius, C. L. (2024). What Impacts Can We Expect from School Spending Policy? Evidence from Evaluations in the United States. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 16(1). Spending raises test scores and college-going on average.

title: Zoning & Housing Supply
text:
Housing supply elasticity determines how prices respond to demand shocks. When demand increases (population growth, rising incomes, low interest rates), the outcome depends entirely on how easily builders can add new housing:

Elastic supply (few regulations, available land): builders respond to higher demand by constructing more units. Prices stay relatively stable. Think Houston, Dallas, Atlanta.
Inelastic supply (strict zoning, geographic constraints): builders can’t respond. Demand increases → prices spike. Think San Francisco, New York, Boston.

The supply curve is simple:
\[Q^s = \alpha + \eta \cdot P\]
where \(\eta\) is the supply elasticity. When \(\eta\) is large, quantity responds easily to price signals. When \(\eta\) is small, prices bear the full burden of demand shifts.


Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks (2005) showed that in highly regulated cities, housing prices far exceed physical construction costs. The gap — what they call the regulatory tax — is the implicit cost of zoning, permitting delays, building height restrictions, and neighborhood opposition (NIMBYism).
In Manhattan, the regulatory tax can exceed $100,000 per apartment. In Houston, it’s close to zero. The difference is not construction technology — it’s regulation.



Saiz (2010) estimated housing supply elasticity for US metro areas, finding enormous variation:



City
Supply Elasticity




Houston
~2.3 (very elastic)


Atlanta
~2.5


Chicago
~0.8


Boston
~0.8


San Francisco
~0.6 (very inelastic)


Miami
~0.6



Geographic constraints (water, mountains) and regulatory constraints both contribute. San Francisco has both — water on three sides and strict zoning.






The Model View. The simulation below uses linear supply and demand curves. In reality, supply curves are kinked — elastic at low prices (easy to build) but becoming inelastic as land runs out or regulations bind. The key intuition holds: inelastic supply amplifies price volatility.

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  market <- reactive({
    eta <- input$elasticity
    d0 <- input$demand0
    shock_pct <- input$shock / 100
    c_cost <- input$cost
    rent_ctrl <- input$rent_control

    # Demand curve: P = a - b*Q
    # Higher d0 shifts demand right
    a_init <- d0 * 4
    b_dem <- 1.5

    # Supply curve: P = c_cost + (1/eta)*Q
    # Higher eta = flatter supply

    # Initial equilibrium: a_init - b_dem*Q = c_cost + Q/eta
    # Q* = (a_init - c_cost) / (b_dem + 1/eta)
    q_init <- (a_init - c_cost) / (b_dem + 1 / eta)
    q_init <- max(q_init, 1)
    p_init <- c_cost + q_init / eta

    # After demand shock: demand shifts right
    a_new <- a_init * (1 + shock_pct)
    q_new <- (a_new - c_cost) / (b_dem + 1 / eta)
    q_new <- max(q_new, 1)
    p_new <- c_cost + q_new / eta

    # With rent control: price stays at p_init, shortage develops
    if (rent_ctrl && shock_pct > 0) {
      p_ctrl <- p_init
      q_supplied_ctrl <- (p_ctrl - c_cost) * eta  # supply at controlled price
      q_demanded_ctrl <- (a_new - p_ctrl) / b_dem  # demand at controlled price
      shortage <- q_demanded_ctrl - q_supplied_ctrl
    } else {
      p_ctrl <- p_new
      q_supplied_ctrl <- q_new
      q_demanded_ctrl <- q_new
      shortage <- 0
    }

    # Regulatory tax
    reg_tax <- p_new - c_cost

    # Price change
    price_change_pct <- (p_new - p_init) / p_init * 100
    quantity_change_pct <- (q_new - q_init) / q_init * 100

    # Affordability (price / income proxy)
    income <- d0 * 0.8  # rough income proxy
    afford_init <- p_init / income
    afford_new <- p_new / income

    list(q_init = q_init, p_init = p_init,
         q_new = q_new, p_new = p_new,
         a_init = a_init, a_new = a_new,
         b_dem = b_dem, eta = eta, c_cost = c_cost,
         reg_tax = reg_tax,
         price_change = price_change_pct,
         quantity_change = quantity_change_pct,
         afford_init = afford_init, afford_new = afford_new,
         rent_ctrl = rent_ctrl, shortage = shortage,
         p_ctrl = p_ctrl, q_supplied_ctrl = q_supplied_ctrl,
         q_demanded_ctrl = q_demanded_ctrl,
         shock_pct = shock_pct)
  })

  output$sd_plot <- renderPlot({
    m <- market()
    par(mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))

    q_max <- max(m$q_new, m$q_init, m$q_demanded_ctrl, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.4
    p_max <- max(m$p_new, m$p_init, m$a_new) * 1.1

    q_range <- seq(0, q_max, length.out = 200)

    # Supply curve
    p_supply <- m$c_cost + q_range / m$eta

    # Demand curves
    p_demand_init <- m$a_init - m$b_dem * q_range
    p_demand_new <- m$a_new - m$b_dem * q_range

    plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, q_max), ylim = c(0, p_max),
         xlab = "Quantity (housing units)",
         ylab = "Price ($1000s)",
         main = "Housing Supply and Demand")

    # Supply
    lines(q_range, p_supply, lwd = 3, col = "#e74c3c")

    # Initial demand
    lines(q_range[p_demand_init > 0], p_demand_init[p_demand_init > 0],
          lwd = 2, col = "#3498db", lty = 2)

    # New demand (if shock > 0)
    if (m$shock_pct > 0) {
      lines(q_range[p_demand_new > 0], p_demand_new[p_demand_new > 0],
            lwd = 3, col = "#3498db")
    }

    # Construction cost line
    abline(h = m$c_cost, lty = 3, col = "#95a5a6", lwd = 1.5)
    text(q_max * 0.02, m$c_cost, "Construction cost", pos = 3, cex = 0.75, col = "#95a5a6")

    # Initial equilibrium
    points(m$q_init, m$p_init, pch = 19, cex = 2, col = "#7f8c8d")

    # New equilibrium
    if (m$shock_pct > 0) {
      if (m$rent_ctrl) {
        # Show rent control price and shortage
        abline(h = m$p_ctrl, lty = 2, col = "#f39c12", lwd = 2)
        text(q_max * 0.5, m$p_ctrl, "Rent control ceiling", pos = 3,
             cex = 0.85, col = "#f39c12", font = 2)

        # Shortage bracket
        arrows(m$q_supplied_ctrl, m$p_ctrl * 0.92,
               m$q_demanded_ctrl, m$p_ctrl * 0.92,

title: Zoning & Housing Supply
text:
Housing supply elasticity determines how prices respond to demand shocks. When demand increases (population growth, rising incomes, low interest rates), the outcome depends entirely on how easily builders can add new housing:

Elastic supply (few regulations, available land): builders respond to higher demand by constructing more units. Prices stay relatively stable. Think Houston, Dallas, Atlanta.
Inelastic supply (strict zoning, geographic constraints): builders can’t respond. Demand increases → prices spike. Think San Francisco, New York, Boston.

The supply curve is simple:
\[Q^s = \alpha + \eta \cdot P\]
where \(\eta\) is the supply elasticity. When \(\eta\) is large, quantity responds easily to price signals. When \(\eta\) is small, prices bear the full burden of demand shifts.


Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks (2005) showed that in highly regulated cities, housing prices far exceed physical construction costs. The gap — what they call the regulatory tax — is the implicit cost of zoning, permitting delays, building height restrictions, and neighborhood opposition (NIMBYism).
In Manhattan, the regulatory tax can exceed $100,000 per apartment. In Houston, it’s close to zero. The difference is not construction technology — it’s regulation.



Saiz (2010) estimated housing supply elasticity for US metro areas, finding enormous variation:



City
Supply Elasticity




Houston
~2.3 (very elastic)


Atlanta
~2.5


Chicago
~0.8


Boston
~0.8


San Francisco
~0.6 (very inelastic)


Miami
~0.6



Geographic constraints (water, mountains) and regulatory constraints both contribute. San Francisco has both — water on three sides and strict zoning.






The Model View. The simulation below uses linear supply and demand curves. In reality, supply curves are kinked — elastic at low prices (easy to build) but becoming inelastic as land runs out or regulations bind. The key intuition holds: inelastic supply amplifies price volatility.

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  market <- reactive({
    eta <- input$elasticity
    d0 <- input$demand0
    shock_pct <- input$shock / 100
    c_cost <- input$cost
    rent_ctrl <- input$rent_control

    # Demand curve: P = a - b*Q
    # Higher d0 shifts demand right
    a_init <- d0 * 4
    b_dem <- 1.5

    # Supply curve: P = c_cost + (1/eta)*Q
    # Higher eta = flatter supply

    # Initial equilibrium: a_init - b_dem*Q = c_cost + Q/eta
    # Q* = (a_init - c_cost) / (b_dem + 1/eta)
    q_init <- (a_init - c_cost) / (b_dem + 1 / eta)
    q_init <- max(q_init, 1)
    p_init <- c_cost + q_init / eta

    # After demand shock: demand shifts right
    a_new <- a_init * (1 + shock_pct)
    q_new <- (a_new - c_cost) / (b_dem + 1 / eta)
    q_new <- max(q_new, 1)
    p_new <- c_cost + q_new / eta

    # With rent control: price stays at p_init, shortage develops
    if (rent_ctrl && shock_pct > 0) {
      p_ctrl <- p_init
      q_supplied_ctrl <- (p_ctrl - c_cost) * eta  # supply at controlled price
      q_demanded_ctrl <- (a_new - p_ctrl) / b_dem  # demand at controlled price
      shortage <- q_demanded_ctrl - q_supplied_ctrl
    } else {
      p_ctrl <- p_new
      q_supplied_ctrl <- q_new
      q_demanded_ctrl <- q_new
      shortage <- 0
    }

    # Regulatory tax
    reg_tax <- p_new - c_cost

    # Price change
    price_change_pct <- (p_new - p_init) / p_init * 100
    quantity_change_pct <- (q_new - q_init) / q_init * 100

    # Affordability (price / income proxy)
    income <- d0 * 0.8  # rough income proxy
    afford_init <- p_init / income
    afford_new <- p_new / income

    list(q_init = q_init, p_init = p_init,
         q_new = q_new, p_new = p_new,
         a_init = a_init, a_new = a_new,
         b_dem = b_dem, eta = eta, c_cost = c_cost,
         reg_tax = reg_tax,
         price_change = price_change_pct,
         quantity_change = quantity_change_pct,
         afford_init = afford_init, afford_new = afford_new,
         rent_ctrl = rent_ctrl, shortage = shortage,
         p_ctrl = p_ctrl, q_supplied_ctrl = q_supplied_ctrl,
         q_demanded_ctrl = q_demanded_ctrl,
         shock_pct = shock_pct)
  })

  output$sd_plot <- renderPlot({
    m <- market()
    par(mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))

    q_max <- max(m$q_new, m$q_init, m$q_demanded_ctrl, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.4
    p_max <- max(m$p_new, m$p_init, m$a_new) * 1.1

    q_range <- seq(0, q_max, length.out = 200)

    # Supply curve
    p_supply <- m$c_cost + q_range / m$eta

    # Demand curves
    p_demand_init <- m$a_init - m$b_dem * q_range
    p_demand_new <- m$a_new - m$b_dem * q_range

    plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, q_max), ylim = c(0, p_max),
         xlab = "Quantity (housing units)",
         ylab = "Price ($1000s)",
         main = "Housing Supply and Demand")

    # Supply
    lines(q_range, p_supply, lwd = 3, col = "#e74c3c")

    # Initial demand
    lines(q_range[p_demand_init > 0], p_demand_init[p_demand_init > 0],
          lwd = 2, col = "#3498db", lty = 2)

    # New demand (if shock > 0)
    if (m$shock_pct > 0) {
      lines(q_range[p_demand_new > 0], p_demand_new[p_demand_new > 0],
            lwd = 3, col = "#3498db")
    }

    # Construction cost line
    abline(h = m$c_cost, lty = 3, col = "#95a5a6", lwd = 1.5)
    text(q_max * 0.02, m$c_cost, "Construction cost", pos = 3, cex = 0.75, col = "#95a5a6")

    # Initial equilibrium
    points(m$q_init, m$p_init, pch = 19, cex = 2, col = "#7f8c8d")

    # New equilibrium
    if (m$shock_pct > 0) {
      if (m$rent_ctrl) {
        # Show rent control price and shortage
        abline(h = m$p_ctrl, lty = 2, col = "#f39c12", lwd = 2)
        text(q_max * 0.5, m$p_ctrl, "Rent control ceiling", pos = 3,
             cex = 0.85, col = "#f39c12", font = 2)

        # Shortage bracket
        arrows(m$q_supplied_ctrl, m$p_ctrl * 0.92,
               m$q_demanded_ctrl, m$p_ctrl * 0.92,
               code = 3, lwd = 2, col = "#e74c3c", length = 0.1)

             paste0("Reg. tax\n$", round(m$reg_tax, 0), "k"),
             cex = 0.8, col = "#8e44ad", font = 2)
      }
    }

    legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.85,
           legend = c("Supply", "Initial demand", "New demand",
                      "Initial eq.", "New eq."),
           col = c("#e74c3c", "#3498db", "#3498db", "#7f8c8d", "#2c3e50"),
           lwd = c(3, 2, 3, NA, NA), lty = c(1, 2, 1, NA, NA),
           pch = c(NA, NA, NA, 19, 19), pt.cex = 2)
  })

  output$info <- renderUI({
    m <- market()

    tags$div(class = "info-box",
      HTML(paste0(
        "<b>Price change:</b> ",
        ifelse(abs(m$price_change) < 1,
               "<span class='good'>+", "<span class='bad'>+"),
        round(m$price_change, 1), "%</span><br>",
        "<b>Quantity change:</b> +", round(m$quantity_change, 1), "%<br>",

        if (m$rent_ctrl && m$shock_pct > 0)
          paste0("<b>Shortage:</b> <span class='bad'>", round(m$shortage, 0), " units</span>")
        else ""

    )
  })
}

title: Zoning & Housing Supply
text:
The housing affordability crisis
The divergence in housing supply elasticity across US cities has enormous consequences. Since the 1970s, coastal cities with inelastic supply (San Francisco, New York, Boston, LA) have seen housing prices dramatically outpace incomes. Interior cities with elastic supply (Houston, Dallas, Phoenix, Atlanta) have not.
This isn’t about demand differences — all these cities experienced income growth and population growth. The difference is supply response. When demand rises and supply can’t respond, prices absorb everything.
Hsieh and Moretti (2019) estimated that housing constraints in high-productivity cities like New York and San Francisco caused a massive spatial misallocation of labor. Workers who would be more productive in these cities can’t afford to live there, so they stay in lower-productivity locations. Their estimate: roughly 36% of US GDP growth between 1964 and 2009 was lost to this misallocation. Later work has debated the size of this number, but not the direction. Relaxing housing constraints in just New York, San Francisco, and San Jose to the median US level would have raised GDP growth substantially.
The policy implication is stark: local zoning decisions have national macroeconomic consequences.

title: Zoning & Housing Supply
text:
Did you know?

Houston is the largest US city with no formal zoning ordinance. Instead, it uses deed restrictions and minimum lot-size requirements. The result: Houston has some of the most affordable housing among large US metros, with median home prices roughly one-third those of San Francisco.
Japan takes a radically different approach: zoning is set nationally, not locally. The national government defines 12 zone types, and local municipalities cannot restrict land use beyond these categories. This means NIMBYs can’t block new housing at the neighborhood level.
Hsieh and Moretti’s (2019) estimate of 36% lost GDP growth is one of the most cited, and most debated, numbers in recent urban economics. The mechanism is simple: productive cities can’t grow because they can’t build housing, so workers are stuck in less productive locations. The aggregate output loss is the difference between actual GDP and what GDP would have been with mobile workers and elastic housing supply.

title: Zoning & Housing Supply
text:
Key papers

Glaeser, E. L., Gyourko, J. and Saks, R. (2005). Why Is Manhattan So Expensive? Regulation and the Rise in Housing Prices. Journal of Law and Economics 48(2). The regulatory tax.
Saiz, A. (2010). The Geographic Determinants of Housing Supply. Quarterly Journal of Economics 125(3). Land, geography, and supply elasticities.
Hsieh, C.-T. and Moretti, E. (2019). Housing Constraints and Spatial Misallocation. American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics 11(2). The cost of housing limits to national output.
Büchler, S. and Lutz, E. (2024). Making Housing Affordable? The Local Effects of Relaxing Land-Use Regulation. Journal of Urban Economics 143. Upzoning, new supply, and local rents.

title: GIS Lab 5: Distance Rings Around Crimes
text:
Why it matters
Buyers pay less for homes they expect to be less safe. In Crime and Neighborhoods, we compare crime in a small near ring with crime in a wider far band, so the far band picks up whatever is happening in the whole area. In this lab you draw those rings yourself with real public data. You will also see why a simple map comparison is not enough to measure what crime does to prices.

title: GIS Lab 5: Distance Rings Around Crimes
text:
Data



Source
What to download
Format




DataSF, Police Department Incident Reports: 2018 to Present
Burglaries reported in 2023, with coordinates. This link downloads exactly that: burglaries_2023.csv (about 6,700 rows)
CSV with latitude and longitude


Census Reporter, Median Value (Dollars), table B25077 for San Francisco census tracts (American Community Survey, 5-year estimates)
Click Download data, then Shapefile. The file includes the tract boundaries.
Shapefile (zip). Key field: B25077001 = median home value



Ready-made zip: [ZIP PLACEHOLDER]
Notes on the data.

The incident data are reports to the San Francisco Police Department. Not every crime is reported.
ACS home values are self-reported by owners and averaged over five years. Values of $2,000,001 mean “two million or more”: the ACS does not report higher values.

title: GIS Lab 5: Distance Rings Around Crimes
text:
Software

QGIS 3.44 LTR (free, from qgis.org). Menu names below are from 3.44. Newer versions may place some tools in different menus. Use the search box in the Processing Toolbox to find any tool by name.
A spreadsheet program (Excel, Google Sheets, or Numbers) for step 10.

title: GIS Lab 5: Distance Rings Around Crimes
text:
Steps

Start a project in meters. Open QGIS and start a new project. Go to Project > Properties > CRS and choose EPSG:26910 (NAD83 / UTM zone 10N). This lets you measure distances in meters.
[SCREENSHOT: Project Properties window with EPSG:26910 selected]
Add the tracts. Unzip the Census Reporter download. Go to Layer > Add Layer > Add Vector Layer and open the .shp file. You should see San Francisco’s census tracts.
[SCREENSHOT: San Francisco tracts loaded as gray polygons]
Add the burglaries. Go to Layer > Add Layer > Add Delimited Text Layer. Choose burglaries_2023.csv. Set X field to longitude, Y field to latitude, and Geometry CRS to EPSG:4326. Click Add.
[SCREENSHOT: Delimited Text dialog with longitude, latitude, and EPSG:4326 filled in]
Put both layers in meters. Open the Processing Toolbox and run Reproject layer twice: once for the tracts and once for the burglaries, both to EPSG:26910. Use the two new layers from now on.
[SCREENSHOT: Reproject layer dialog with target CRS EPSG:26910]
Find the center of each tract. Go to Vector > Geometry Tools > Centroids and run it on the reprojected tracts. Each tract now has one point at its center.
[SCREENSHOT: Tracts with a centroid point in each]
Draw the rings. In the Processing Toolbox, run Multi-ring buffer (constant distance) on the centroids. Set Number of rings to 3 and Distance between rings to 161 meters (0.1 mile). This makes three rings around each center: 0 to 0.1 mile, 0.1 to 0.2 mile, and 0.2 to 0.3 mile.
[SCREENSHOT: Three rings around a few tract centroids]
Keep the near ring and the far band. Run Extract by attribute on the rings twice. First keep ringId = 1 and save it as near_rings (0 to 0.1 mile). Then keep ringId = 3 and save it as far_rings (0.2 to 0.3 mile).
[SCREENSHOT: Extract by attribute dialog with ringId = 1]
Count burglaries in each ring. Go to Vector > Analysis Tools > Count Points in Polygon. Run it on near_rings with the burglaries, and name the count field near_n. Run it again on far_rings and name the count field far_n.
[SCREENSHOT: Attribute table of near_rings showing the near_n column]
Bring the counts back to the tracts and compute rates. Run Join attributes by field value to add near_n to the tracts, matching on geoid. Do it again to add far_n. Then open the Field Calculator on the joined layer and make three new decimal fields:

near_rate = "near_n" / 0.0314 (burglaries per square mile in the near ring)
far_rate = "far_n" / 0.1571 (burglaries per square mile in the far band)
near_minus_far = "near_rate" - "far_rate"

[SCREENSHOT: Field Calculator creating near_rate]
Map it and compare. Color the tracts by B25077001 (Symbology > Graduated, 5 classes) and show the burglaries as small dots on top. Export the map from a Print Layout as a PNG. Then right-click the tract layer, choose Export > Save Features As, and save it as CSV. In a spreadsheet, drop tracts with no home value, split the tracts into thirds by near_rate, and find the median home value in each third.
[SCREENSHOT: Final map with tracts colored by median home value and burglary dots on top]

title: GIS Lab 5: Distance Rings Around Crimes
text:
Hand in
One map (step 10) and a short answer, 3 to 4 sentences for each question:

Where in San Francisco were burglaries most concentrated in 2023?
What is the median home value in the low, middle, and high thirds of near_rate? Are home values lower where more burglaries happened nearby?
Do you reach the same answer if you use near_minus_far instead of near_rate?
Give one reason why this tract-level comparison does not tell us how much crime itself lowers home values. What would a better design compare?

title: GIS Lab 5: Distance Rings Around Crimes
text:
Time
About 45 to 60 minutes.






NoteInstructor notes (click to open)





What students should find. These numbers come from running the steps in Python on the same public files (ACS 2020 to 2024 5-year estimates via Census Reporter, and 2023 burglaries from DataSF, downloaded November 2026). Students’ numbers should be close.

About 6,740 burglaries with coordinates in 2023. 244 tracts, of which 217 have a home value.
Near ring counts: median 5 per tract, and 32 tracts with zero. Far band counts: median 30.
There is almost no relationship between burglaries and home values across tracts. The correlation between median home value and near_rate is about -0.07.
Median home value by thirds of near_rate: low about $1.33M, middle about $1.63M, high about $1.30M. No clear pattern.
Using near_minus_far gives the same answer: no clear pattern.
29 tracts are top-coded at $2,000,001.

This is the point of question 4. Burglaries cluster downtown and in commercial areas, where homes differ in many other ways. ACS values are five-year averages of owners’ own estimates, and the top is cut off. A cross-section of tracts cannot separate crime from everything else about a place. That is why the module’s design compares near and far crime around individual home sales over time.
Common mistakes.

Buffering in EPSG:4326. The distances come out in degrees, and the rings are huge. Check step 1 and step 4.
Making the far band with Buffer and Difference. Difference removes every tract’s inner buffer from every far band, so neighboring rings eat each other. Multi-ring buffer avoids this.
Keeping tracts with no home value, or treating $2,000,001 as an exact value.
Joining on name instead of geoid.
